fetched_contents.text: A new grading system for female sexual dysfunction based on the female sexual function index in Egyptian women: a cross-sectional study Abstract Objective To provide a grading system that accurately reflects the grades of female sexual dysfunction (FSD) severity. Patients and methods A cross-sectional study was conducted in Assiut University Hospital. It included 500 women who answered the Arabic version of the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) after getting their consent. A gradient of FSD severity was created, classifying FSD into five grades: severe, moderate, mild to moderate, mild, and no FSD. Results According to our grading system, FSD was detected in 339 women (67.8 %); Mild FSD in 20.4%, mild to moderate in 41.6%, moderate in 15.3%, and severe in 22.7%. Mean scores of desire show a linear trend of reduction from 3.8 in mild to 3.36 in mild to moderate to 2.25 in moderate and markedly reduced to 2.1 in severe grade. This difference was highly statistically significant (p= 0.002). The same was reported in arousal, orgasm, and satisfaction domains, while in lubrication and pain domains, the difference was not statistically significant. Conclusion In this study, our grading system was complementary to the FSFI. Moreover, it seems to be more practical and useful in grading the severity of FSD. Keywords: Female sexual dysfunction, FSFI, grading, sexual function Introduction Female sexual dysfunction (FSD) is a prevalent health problem1. It is usually manifested by difficulties getting aroused, lubricated, or having an orgasm despite adequate stimulation2. In contrast to male sexual dysfunction, simple measures such as sexual activity cannot be used as an accurate indicator of dysfunction, as women may stay sexually active with their partners while suffering from some degree of sexual dysfunction3. Many methods were developed to evaluate such problems in research and clinical settings. These include structured interviews, questionnaires, and detailed case histories. Questionnaires have become an easy first choice to screen individuals for FSD4. Among these questionnaires, Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI)5 is considered a “gold standard” measure to reflect female sexual function6. This questionnaire was shown to have both high test-retest reliability for each individual domain and a high degree of internal consistency. However, it classifies women into two categories only: normal and abnormal, with a cut-off score of 26.557. An Arabic version of FSFI was later validated by Anis et al.8, who calculated a total score of 28.1 as the cut-off score that defines sexual dysfunction in the Egyptian population. The wide range of total FSFI scores denoting FSD (2-28.1), in addition to the high prevalence of FSD worldwide, highlighted the need for a grading system that can classify women with FSD into several severity levels. Moreover, the variability of FSD therapeutic options, the serious side effects of some of those therapies, and the lack of treatment guidelines for FSD are essential reasons for considering the need for a grading system. Patients and methods This study aimed to provide a grading system for the FSFI that accurately reflects grades of FSD severity and to present data supporting its use as a diagnostically valid instrument in clinical settings worldwide. A cross-sectional hospital-based study was conducted at the outpatient clinics of Dermatology, Venereology, and Andrology department, Assiut University Hospital from June 2016 to August 2017 after obtaining informed consent from all women who agreed to participate in the study and approving the proposal from the local ethical institutional review board. The target women were healthy, sexually active married Egyptian women aged 18 to 55 years who had visited the hospital for a routine check-up or mild dermatological illnesses. It also included women who had accompanied other patients. We excluded women with severe or chronic medical diseases, psychiatric illness, pregnancy, and lactation, and were not sexually active in the last six months. We calculated the sample size according to the equation for the sample size of descriptive study design9; that is: N= {Z2(1-P)P}/D2 where: N: minimum sample size required, Z: standard normal variance=1.96 at 95% confidence interval, D: Absolute standard error that can be tolerated =0.05 and P: prevalence= 50% (based on previous studies in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey)10-12. A sample size of at least 385 women was required to achieve the aim of the study. A total of 500 women were targeted to increase the statistical reliability of the study. Women were interviewed in a private room with their names and addresses not recorded to ensure confidentiality. They were asked to fill out the Arabic version of the FSFI. This 19-item standardized questionnaire covers six domains: desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain. It evaluates sexual function during the last month8. For each domain, a score was calculated, and the total score was obtained by adding the six domain scores. The total score range was 2 to 36. We developed a new grading system for determining the severity of FSD among the studied sample and named it (Sahar's grading system); this system tries to classify the total score obtained by FSDI into several grades, which can reflect its severity as shown in table (1). fetched_contents.text: The Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI): a multidimensional self-report instrument for the assessment of female sexual function J Sex Marital Ther. 2000 Apr-Jun;26(2):191-208. doi: 10.1080/009262300278597. Authors Affiliation * 1 Dept. of Psychiatry, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Piscataway, NJ 08854, USA. * PMID: 10782451 * DOI: 10.1080/009262300278597 Abstract This article presents the development of a brief, self-report measure of female sexual function. Initial face validity testing of questionnaire items, identified by an expert panel, was followed by a study aimed at further refining the questionnaire. It was administered to 131 normal controls and 128 age-matched subjects with female sexual arousal disorder (FSAD) at five research centers. Based on clinical interpretations of a principal components analysis, a 6-domain structure was identified, which included desire, subjective arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain. Overall test-retest reliability coefficients were high for each of the individual domains (r = 0.79 to 0.86) and a high degree of internal consistency was observed (Cronbach's alpha values of 0.82 and higher) Good construct validity was demonstrated by highly significant mean difference scores between the FSAD and control groups for each of the domains (p < or = 0.001). Additionally, divergent validity with a scale of marital satisfaction was observed. These results support the reliability and psychometric (as well as clinical) validity of the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) in the assessment of key dimensions of female sexual function in clinical and nonclinical samples. Branch report on how the FSFI is scored

The FSFI is scored through a multi-step computational process that begins with item scoring, then domain scoring, and finally total score calculation. The instrument’s scoring system is designed to convert raw item responses into a standardized total score, with domain-specific scaling to allow meaningful comparison across the six domains.

### Mathematical steps used to calculate the total score
The total score is obtained by summing the six domain scores. Within each domain, item scores are summed and then multiplied by a domain factor to convert the raw item sum into a domain-specific score. The full-scale score is then derived by adding the six domain scores together. The APTA source explicitly states: “Individual domain scores are obtained by adding the scores of the individual items that comprise the domain and multiplying the sum by the domain factor” and “the full scale score is obtained by adding the six domain scores” [N1-F1]. The appendix-style scoring table also explains the same logic, indicating that the individual domain scores and full-scale score are derived from the computational formula outlined in the table [N1-R3]. A second source confirms that the full scale score is obtained by adding the six domain scores and notes that a domain score of zero indicates no sexual activity was reported during the past month [N2-R1].

### How missing or invalid responses are handled
The evidence provided does not directly specify how missing or invalid responses are handled in the standard FSFI scoring rules. However, the instrument is administered with explicit response options for each item, and the scoring process assumes that responses are provided for all items relevant to the domain. The APTA source provides the full set of response options for several items, including frequency, confidence, satisfaction, and difficulty ratings [N1-F1], suggesting that the instrument is designed to be completed as a single administration. The scoring instructions also indicate that domain scores are based on the sum of item scores, implying that missing responses may disrupt the sum and therefore the domain score unless handled separately. Since the evidence does not explicitly describe handling of missing or invalid items, this is a limitation of the provided material rather than a definitive rule in the current evidence set [N2-R1][N1-F1].

### What score ranges mean clinically and how they are interpreted
The score range for the FSFI is described as spanning from 2 to 36 in the Egyptian study, with the total score obtained by adding the six domain scores [N2-F2]. The same source also reports that the total score range was 2 to 36 and that a grading system classified FSD severity into five grades: severe, moderate, mild to moderate, mild, and no FSD [N2-F2]. In the clinical validation paper, the instrument is described as a multidimensional self-report measure with high reliability and validity, and it supports interpretation through domain scores and the total score [N3-F3]. However, the evidence provided here does not give a universal clinical interpretation for all scores across all populations; instead, it shows that the instrument can be interpreted using a cut-off score of 26.5 or other locally validated thresholds [N2-F2]. The review article emphasizes that the FSFI is used to calculate a total sexual functioning score, but it also notes that this is appropriate only when participants have engaged in sexual activity and have attempted vaginal penetration [N2-R3]. That implies that score interpretation should be contextual and may vary across settings.

### Summary of scoring logic
In short, the FSFI score is computed by:
1. Summing item scores for each domain,
2. Multiplying the item sum by the domain factor to obtain the domain score,
3. Adding the six domain scores to produce the full-scale score [N1-F1][N1-R3].
The score range is typically 2–36, but interpretation depends on population-specific cut-offs and local validation [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence provided here does not fully specify handling of missing responses, so that aspect remains under-supported in the current materials [N2-R1][N1-F1].

Branch report on evidence and limitations of the FSFI

The FSFI has strong psychometric support, but it also has recognized limitations that are important for interpretation.

### Major reliability and validity evidence supporting the FSFI
The strongest evidence comes from the original development paper, which reported that the instrument was administered to 131 normal controls and 128 age-matched subjects with female sexual arousal disorder (FSAD) [N3-F3]. The paper found that the 6-domain structure included desire, subjective arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain [N3-F3]. It also reported high test-retest reliability coefficients for each domain (r = 0.79 to 0.86) and high internal consistency with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.82 and higher [N3-F3]. Construct validity was demonstrated by highly significant mean difference scores between the FSAD and control groups for each domain (p < 0.001) [N3-F3]. A separate source reinforces that Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.82 and higher were found, and good construct validity was demonstrated with divergent validity relative to marital satisfaction [N3-R2]. Another source states that all FSFI scores had very high reliability and that the Cronbach α value for the total score was .94 (95% CI .92–.95) [N3-R5]. This suggests strong internal consistency and strong support for the instrument’s validity as a multidimensional measure of female sexual function [N3-F3][N3-R5].

### Known limitations or criticisms of the instrument
The most direct criticism is that the FSFI is not appropriate for individuals who are not currently sexually active, and research with a focus other than sexual arousal should consider supplementary measures [N5-F4]. A second source notes that the FSFI and the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF) have potential measurement and psychometric flaws that have not been addressed in the literature [N5-F4]. Specifically, the authors argue that the measures have critical theoretical and measurement problems for assessing sexual problems beyond sexual arousal, and for the sexual desire domains in particular [N5-F4]. These criticisms are reinforced by the point that the measures should be reassessed in clinical samples and that theoretical issues are relevant across clinical and research contexts [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that the FSFI is inappropriate for use among individuals who are not currently sexually active, which is an important limitation because the instrument is based on a sexual activity frame [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The provided evidence does not specify how common these limitations are in practice, but it does establish that they are serious concerns for validity and interpretation [N5-F4][N5-R1].

### How the FSFI compares with other sexual functioning measures
The evidence suggests that the FSFI is a widely used, multidimensional, self-report instrument, and it is often positioned as a “gold standard” measure of female sexual function [N3-F3][N2-F2]. However, it is not the only measure available. The same source contrasts the FSFI with other sexual functioning assessments by noting that the FSFI was developed as a brief self-report measure of female sexual function and that the original study compared it with a control group of women with FSAD [N3-F3]. Another source explicitly states that the FSFI is a patient-reported outcome measure measuring female sexual dysfunction [N5-R4]. The criticisms provided in the literature indicate that the FSFI should not be used as a standalone measure in contexts beyond sexual arousal or in populations not engaged in sexual activity [N5-F4]. In short, the FSFI is a strong, validated instrument, but it is not universally interchangeable with other sexual functioning measures because of its domain specificity and potential limitations in non-sexually active or multi-domain assessment contexts [N3-F3][N3-R5][N5-F4].

### Conclusion
The FSFI has strong reliability and validity evidence, including high internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity [N3-F3][N3-R5]. Its main limitations are that it may not be suitable for non-sexually active individuals and that it has theoretical and measurement concerns for assessing sexual problems beyond sexual arousal and sexual desire [N5-F4][N5-R1]. Overall, it is a well-supported instrument, but its use should be complemented by other measures when appropriate [N5-F4].

The FSFI has been adapted across cultures and contexts. The evidence includes a transculturally adapted version of the instrument [N4-R3], which supports its use in different cultural settings. ### Conclusion
The FSFI is a widely used and clinically relevant instrument, commonly applied in both research and clinical settings for assessing female sexual functioning and dysfunction [N1-R4][N3-F3]. The instrument has also been adapted across cultures, including an Arabic version validated for use in Egypt [N2-F2], but adaptation must be done carefully and validated locally [N4-R3].

It is structured around six domains and 19 items, with a scoring system that combines item-level responses into domain scores and then into a total score. The instrument is intended to capture multiple aspects of sexual function, including desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-F3]. Below is an integrated explanation of its design and scoring.

## 1. Design: a multidimensional self-report questionnaire

### Six domains and items
The FSFI is organized into **six domains**: desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-F3]. The evidence also provides the item distribution across domains:
- Desire: questions 1 and 2
- Arousal: questions 3, 4, 5, and 6

- Orgasm: questions 11, 12, and 13
- Satisfaction: questions 14, 15, and 16
- Pain: questions 17, 18, and 19 [N1-F1]

This structure reflects the instrument’s goal of assessing sexual functioning across key dimensions rather than relying on a single global score. The original development paper describes the six-domain structure as a result of clinical interpretations of a principal components analysis [N3-F3].

### Item construction and administration format
The FSFI is a **self-report questionnaire**. The APTA source provides the full set of response options and instructions, indicating that the instrument asks about sexual feelings and responses during the past 4 weeks and that participants are instructed to answer honestly [N6-R2]. The response options are standardized across items and vary by question type:
- Frequency ratings: “Almost always or always,” “Most times,” “Sometimes,” “A few times,” “Almost never or never”
- Confidence/rating scales: “Very high confidence,” “High confidence,” “Moderate confidence,” “Low confidence,” “Very low or no confidence”
- Satisfaction ratings: “Very satisfied,” “Moderately satisfied,” “About equally satisfied and dissatisfied,” “Moderately dissatisfied,” “Very dissatisfied”
- Difficulty ratings: “Extremely difficult or impossible,” “Very difficult,” “Difficult,” “Slightly difficult,” “Not difficult”
- Response options for pain: “Very high,” “High,” “Moderate,” “Low,” “Very low or none at all” [N1-F1]

The administration format is therefore clearly a **questionnaire-based self-report** rather than a clinical interview. The evidence does not explicitly describe a digital or paper-based administration format, but the repeated use of standardized response options and instructions supports the conclusion that the instrument is administered as a completed questionnaire [N6-R1][N6-R2].

---

## 2. Scoring: a multi-step process from item to total score

### Mathematical steps used to calculate the total score
The FSFI is scored in three steps:
1. **Item scores are summed within each domain**
2. **The sum is multiplied by a domain factor to obtain the domain score**
3. **The six domain scores are added together to produce the full-scale score**

The APTA source explains: “Individual domain scores are obtained by adding the scores of the individual items that comprise the domain and multiplying the sum by the domain factor” [N1-F1]. The same source also states that the full scale score is obtained by adding the six domain scores [N1-F1]. In the Egyptian study, a grading system classified FSD severity into five grades: severe, moderate, mild to moderate, mild, and no FSD [N2-F2]. This shows that the instrument is often interpreted using a **cut-off or severity classification** framework, though the exact interpretation may vary by population and context.

The review article also notes that using the FSFI to calculate a total sexual functioning score is appropriate only when participants have engaged in sexual activity and have attempted vaginal penetration [N2-R3]. This means that the clinical interpretation of the total score should be context-sensitive and may not be valid for non-sexually active women or for settings where sexual activity is not the focus.

### How missing or invalid responses are handled
The evidence provided here does **not** explicitly specify a standardized handling rule for missing or invalid responses. However, the instrument is administered with explicit response options for each item, and the scoring process assumes that responses are provided for all relevant items [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Because the domain score depends on summing item scores, missing responses could disrupt the sum and therefore the domain score unless handled separately. Since the evidence does not describe missing-data handling, that aspect remains under-supported in the current materials [N2-R1][N1-F1].

## 3. Evidence supporting the FSFI

### Major reliability and validity evidence
The FSFI has strong psychometric support. The original development paper reports high **test-retest reliability** for each domain (r = 0.79 to 0.86) and high **internal consistency** with **Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.82 and higher** [N3-F3]. ### How the FSFI compares with other sexual functioning measures
The evidence suggests that the FSFI is a widely used, multidimensional, self-report instrument, and it is often positioned as a “gold standard” measure of female sexual function [N3-F3][N2-F2]. However, it is not the only measure available. The same source contrasts the FSFI with other sexual functioning assessments by noting that the FSFI was developed as a brief self-report measure of female sexual function and that the original study compared it with a control group of women with FSAD [N3-F3]. The criticisms provided in the literature indicate that the FSFI should not be used as a standalone measure in contexts beyond sexual arousal or in populations not engaged in sexual activity [N5-F4]. The FSFI has strong reliability and validity evidence, including high internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity [N3-F3][N3-R5]. Its main limitations are that it may not be suitable for non-sexually active individuals and that it has theoretical and measurement concerns for assessing sexual problems beyond sexual arousal and sexual desire [N5-F4][N5-R1]. Overall, it is a well-supported instrument, but its use should be complemented by other measures when appropriate [N5-F4].

## How the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) is designed and scored to provide a comprehensive assessment of women’s sexual functioning

The Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) is a widely used, multidimensional self-report questionnaire designed to provide a comprehensive assessment of women’s sexual functioning. It is structured around six domains and 19 items, with a scoring system that combines item-level responses into domain scores and then into a total score. The instrument is intended to capture multiple aspects of sexual function, including desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-F3]. Below is an integrated explanation of its design and scoring.

---

## 1. Design: a multidimensional self-report questionnaire

### Six domains and items
The FSFI is organized into **six domains**: desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-F3]. The evidence also provides the item distribution across domains:
- Desire: questions 1 and 2
- Arousal: questions 3, 4, 5, and 6
- Lubrication: questions 7, 8, 9, and 10
- Orgasm: questions 11, 12, and 13
- Satisfaction: questions 14, 15, and 16
- Pain: questions 17, 18, and 19 [N1-F1]

This structure reflects the instrument’s goal of assessing sexual functioning across key dimensions rather than relying on a single global score. The original development paper describes the six-domain structure as a result of clinical interpretations of a principal components analysis [N3-F3].

### Item construction and administration format
The FSFI is a **self-report questionnaire**. The APTA source provides the full set of response options and instructions, indicating that the instrument asks about sexual feelings and responses during the past 4 weeks and that participants are instructed to answer honestly [N6-R2]. The response options are standardized across items and vary by question type:
- Frequency ratings: “Almost always or always,” “Most times,” “Sometimes,” “A few times,” “Almost never or never”
- Confidence/rating scales: “Very high confidence,” “High confidence,” “Moderate confidence,” “Low confidence,” “Very low or no confidence”
- Satisfaction ratings: “Very satisfied,” “Moderately satisfied,” “About equally satisfied and dissatisfied,” “Moderately dissatisfied,” “Very dissatisfied”
- Difficulty ratings: “Extremely difficult or impossible,” “Very difficult,” “Difficult,” “Slightly difficult,” “Not difficult”
- Response options for pain: “Very high,” “High,” “Moderate,” “Low,” “Very low or none at all” [N1-F1]

The administration format is therefore clearly a **questionnaire-based self-report** rather than a clinical interview. The evidence does not explicitly describe a digital or paper-based administration format, but the repeated use of standardized response options and instructions supports the conclusion that the instrument is administered as a completed questionnaire [N6-R1][N6-R2].

---

## 2. Scoring: a multi-step process from item to total score

### Mathematical steps used to calculate the total score
The FSFI is scored in three steps:
1. **Item scores are summed within each domain**
2. **The sum is multiplied by a domain factor to obtain the domain score**
3. **The six domain scores are added together to produce the full-scale score**

The APTA source explains: “Individual domain scores are obtained by adding the scores of the individual items that comprise the domain and multiplying the sum by the domain factor” [N1-F1]. The same source also states that the full scale score is obtained by adding the six domain scores [N1-F1]. The appendix-style scoring table explicitly describes the computational formula used to derive the individual domain scores and the full-scale score [N1-R3].

### What score ranges mean clinically and how they are interpreted
The score range is typically **2–36**, based on the Egyptian study, where the total score was derived from adding the six domain scores and the total score range was 2 to 36 [N2-F2]. In the Egyptian study, a grading system classified FSD severity into five grades: severe, moderate, mild to moderate, mild, and no FSD [N2-F2]. This shows that the instrument is often interpreted using a **cut-off or severity classification** framework, though the exact interpretation may vary by population and context.

The review article also notes that using the FSFI to calculate a total sexual functioning score is appropriate only when participants have engaged in sexual activity and have attempted vaginal penetration [N2-R3]. This means that the clinical interpretation of the total score should be context-sensitive and may not be valid for non-sexually active women or for settings where sexual activity is not the focus.

### How missing or invalid responses are handled
The evidence provided here does **not** explicitly specify a standardized handling rule for missing or invalid responses. However, the instrument is administered with explicit response options for each item, and the scoring process assumes that responses are provided for all relevant items [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Because the domain score depends on summing item scores, missing responses could disrupt the sum and therefore the domain score unless handled separately. Since the evidence does not describe missing-data handling, that aspect remains under-supported in the current materials [N2-R1][N1-F1].

---

## 3. Evidence supporting the FSFI

### Major reliability and validity evidence
The FSFI has strong psychometric support. The original development paper reports high **test-retest reliability** for each domain (r = 0.79 to 0.86) and high **internal consistency** with **Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.82 and higher** [N3-F3]. It also demonstrates **construct validity** through highly significant mean difference scores between women with female sexual arousal disorder (FSAD) and controls for each domain (p < 0.001) [N3-F3]. A separate source reinforces that Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.82 and higher were found, and good construct validity was demonstrated with divergent validity relative to marital satisfaction [N3-R2]. Another source reports that all FSFI scores had **very high reliability** and that the total-score Cronbach α was .94 (95% CI .92–.95) [N3-R5].

The instrument is also described as a “gold standard” measure for female sexual function in research and clinical settings [N3-F3][N2-F2]. It is further noted as a multidimensional self-report measure with strong reliability and validity [N3-F3].

### How the FSFI compares with other sexual functioning measures
The evidence suggests that the FSFI is a widely used, multidimensional, self-report instrument, and it is often positioned as a **gold standard** measure of female sexual function [N3-F3][N2-F2]. However, it is not the only measure available. The same source contrasts the FSFI with other sexual functioning assessments by noting that the FSFI was developed as a brief self-report measure of female sexual function [N3-F3]. Another source explicitly describes the FSFI as a patient-reported outcome measure measuring female sexual dysfunction [N5-R4].

The criticisms in the literature indicate that the FSFI should not be used as a standalone measure in contexts beyond sexual arousal or in populations not engaged in sexual activity [N5-F4]. This means that while the FSFI is a strong, validated instrument, it is not universally interchangeable with other sexual functioning measures in all contexts.

---

## 4. Limitations and criticisms of the FSFI

### Known limitations
The most direct criticism is that the FSFI is **not appropriate for individuals who are not currently sexually active**, and research with a focus other than sexual arousal should consider supplementary measures [N5-F4]. A second source notes that the FSFI and the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF) have **potential measurement and psychometric flaws** that have not been fully addressed in the literature [N5-F4]. Specifically, the authors argue that the measures have **critical theoretical and measurement problems** for assessing sexual problems beyond sexual arousal, and for the sexual desire domains in particular [N5-F4].

The evidence also notes that the FSFI is **inappropriate for use among individuals who are not currently sexually active** [N5-R1][N5-R3]. This is an important limitation because the instrument is based on a sexual activity frame: the scoring instructions state that a domain score of zero indicates that **no sexual activity was reported during the past month** [N2-R1].

### How these limitations affect interpretation
Because the FSFI depends on reports of sexual activity and sexual experiences, its interpretation is **context-dependent**. The Egyptian study’s grading system shows how the instrument can be used to classify FSD severity, but it also highlights that the same score range may not apply uniformly across populations [N2-F2]. The review article further notes that the FSFI is appropriate only when participants have engaged in sexual activity and have attempted vaginal penetration, which means the instrument may not be suitable for non-sexually active women or for populations where sexual activity is not the focus of study [N2-R3][N5-F4].

---

## 5. Practical use and populations for which the FSFI is suitable

### Clinical and research settings
The FSFI is commonly used in both **clinical and research settings**. It has been used to assess the effects of interventions in women with female sexual dysfunction, including pharmacological and psychological treatments [N4-R5]. It is also used as a brief multidimensional scale for assessing sexual function in women [N1-R4]. In clinical settings, it is used for screening, severity classification, and monitoring [N2-F2]. The Egyptian study reports that an Arabic version of the FSFI was validated and used to classify FSD severity into five grades [N2-F2], which is a clear example of clinical application.

### Which populations are appropriate or problematic for use
The FSFI is generally appropriate for **adult women**, particularly **sexually active women** [N1-R5]. However, it is problematic for **non-sexually active individuals** because the instrument is based on reports of sexual activity and sexual experiences [N5-F4][N5-R1]. It may also be less suitable for research or clinical contexts that require assessment beyond sexual arousal or desire [N5-F4].

### Adaptation across cultures and contexts
The FSFI has been adapted across cultures and contexts. The evidence includes a **transculturally adapted version** of the instrument [N4-R3]. The Egyptian study reports an **Arabic version** that was validated and used to create a grading system for FSD severity [N2-F2]. This indicates that the instrument can be translated and culturally adapted, but the evidence also suggests that such adaptation must be done carefully and validated locally [N2-F2][N4-R3].

---

## 6. Summary

The FSFI is a **multidimensional, self-report questionnaire** with six domains: desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-F3]. It is scored through a multi-step process: item scores are summed within each domain, multiplied by a domain factor, and then added to produce the total score [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The total score typically ranges from **2 to 36** [N2-F2], but interpretation depends on population-specific cut-offs and local validation [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The instrument has strong **reliability and validity evidence**, including high internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity [N3-F3][N3-R5]. However, it has notable **limitations**: it may not be suitable for non-sexually active individuals, and it may not fully capture sexual problems beyond sexual arousal and sexual desire [N5-F4][N5-R1]. It is therefore best used as part of a broader assessment strategy rather than as a standalone measure in all contexts [N5-F4].

In practice, the FSFI is widely used in **clinical and research settings** to assess female sexual functioning and dysfunction [N1-R4][N3-F3], but it is most appropriate for **sexually active adult women** and should be adapted and validated in different cultural contexts [N4-R3][N2-F2]. Overall, the FSFI is a well-supported instrument for comprehensive assessment, but its design and scoring also impose important interpretive boundaries [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
